summary: For ages 9–11: learners come to understand that no country's ownership of Antarctica is recognised (seven countries have claims, but the Treaty froze them), that the Antarctic Treaty (signed 1959, in force 1961, now 50+ parties) reserves the continent for peaceful, scientific use and bans military activity, that its 1991 Environmental Protocol (in force 1998) adds a ban on mining, and that real science there includes ice-core climate study, dark-sky astronomy, penguin/krill biology and meteorite geology — making it the closest thing on Earth to a continent run for science rather than politics. The guidance pairs a labelled research-station exploration (intended to carry the core facts in a vivid setting) with role-play/debate (intended to develop why cooperation matters and is fragile), plus optional recall checks and a system mini-game, each with stated purposes and limits. All activities are untested proposals, not validated interventions, and no source verifies the effectiveness of any chosen medium.
misconceptions: A country owns Antarctica (or the country nearest it) — no nation owns it; claims are set aside under the Treaty
People can mine or drill Antarctica for resources — mining is banned under the Treaty
Anyone can do anything there — activities are restricted to peaceful, scientific ones and are open to inspection
The stations are permanent towns — they are research bases staffed by rotating scientists, not settled cities
The Treaty is guaranteed forever — it depends on continued cooperation and could face pressure as resources tempt nations

activities.title: Explore an Antarctic research base: who owns it and what is studied
steps: Explore a cutaway of an Antarctic research base, examining each facility in turn.
At the ice-core lab, note how scientists read ancient climate from air trapped in old ice.
At the rooftop telescope, note why the dark, dry, still polar sky suits astronomy.
At the biology hut, note penguin and krill studies; at the meteorite store, note rocks from space found on the ice.

Open a flag-map showing the research stations run by about 30 nations (more than 50 countries have joined the Treaty) and answer 'Who owns Antarctica?' before revealing the answer: no one's ownership is recognised — seven countries have claims, but the 1959 Treaty froze them and keeps the continent for peaceful science with no armies, and a later 1991 agreement (the Environmental Protocol) bans mining.
Consider a follow-up prompt: 'Could that change?' and note the pressure as resources grow tempting.
State in your own words two things the Treaty bans and one kind of science done in Antarctica.
activities.insight: No country's ownership of Antarctica is recognised; the Antarctic Treaty and its later Environmental Protocol reserve the whole continent for peaceful science and ban military activity and mining — an unusual, deliberate act of cooperation that is valuable and fragile.

activities.title: In role: talk to a station scientist and debate the mining ban
steps: Take the role of a visitor speaking with an Antarctic station scientist about daily life on the ice and why no country owns the continent.
Ask why over 50 countries would agree to set aside arguments about who owns land and not to mine there — and what they gain instead (shared, open science).
Debate the question: should the ban on mining ever change? Argue both why keeping it protects a shared space and why pressure to change it grows as resources become tempting.

Respond to a challenge case: a new country wants to join — explain that it must accept the same Treaty rules (no new territorial claims, no military, open inspection), and that most members have also signed the Environmental Protocol, which bans mining.
activities.insight: The Treaty is a shared agreement among nations, not a list handed down by one authority; cooperation over a common space is valuable and can be fragile when resources tempt nations.

activities.title: Check and apply: what the Treaty bans and why
steps: Answer the diagnostic case: a mining company has found valuable metals under Antarctic ice and wants to dig; an army wants to build a base. Are they allowed? Say yes or no, then explain WHICH rule decides.
Recall and match: name two things the Treaty bans and match areas of science (climate, astronomy, biology, geology) to what each studies.

Answer probing extensions: Does building a station and flying a flag mean a country owns that land? What stops the Treaty from being 'just words on paper'? Is the Arctic protected the same way, and why might the North differ from the South?
activities.insight: Antarctica is governed by a shared agreement that bans military use and mining and reserves it for cooperative science — the reason 'no' is given is that all signatory nations agreed, not that any one country is in charge.

activities.title: Optional: run a research station (engagement extension)
steps: Play a short 'run a research station' or 'allocate the science' activity: decide which projects to support (ice cores, telescope time, biology surveys, meteorite collection) and keep operations peaceful and within the rules.
After playing, state which activities the rules allowed and which were off-limits, and why.
activities.insight: Antarctic activity is restricted to peaceful, scientific purposes and is open to inspection — operating a station means working within shared constraints, not doing whatever one wants.

checkQuestion: A mining company says it has found valuable metals under Antarctic ice and wants to dig them up, and an army wants to build a base there. Are they allowed to? Tell me yes or no, and then tell me WHY — what rule decides it?
checkAnswer: No. The Antarctic Treaty (signed 1959, in force since 1961), signed by over 50 countries, sets Antarctica aside for peaceful, scientific purposes only — it bans military activity and mining. So neither the mining company nor the army is allowed; the treaty reserves the whole continent for cooperative science, not national ownership or resource extraction.
